question: What preparations does Adonijah make to reign, who supports him and who is left out of his feast?
The verb שָׁבַע (shava', “swear”) is the argument of Bathsheba and Nathan: what oath do they remind David of, and how does the king respond?
The narrator notes that David had never crossed Adonijah: what relationship does this detail suggest with other crises in David's family?
Adonijah clings to the horns of the altar and Solomon gives him a conditional chance: how do you treat someone who tried to take your place and then grew afraid?
What advice does David give Solomon before he dies, and to what promise does he tie it?
David's last instructions about Joab and Shimei sound like settling scores: how can we reconcile these words with the advice to keep the law of Moses?
The word כִּסֵּא (kisse', “throne”) appears from beginning to end of the chapter: what price does the text show was paid for Solomon's throne to be “firmly established”?
“Be strong and prove yourself a man… keep the charge of the LORD”: what kind of strength does David's advice ask of someone taking on a new responsibility, like you today?
What does God offer Solomon at Gibeon, and how does Solomon describe himself before making his request?
The verb בִּין (bin, “discern, understand”) defines Solomon's request: why is discerning “between good and evil” so necessary for someone who governs a people?
What does the story of the two women show about the kind of wisdom Solomon received?
The chapter begins with the marriage to Pharaoh's daughter and the sacrifices on the high places: why does the narrator place these reservations just before the dream?
If you could ask for just one thing to carry out your current responsibilities well, what would you ask for, and why?
How does Solomon organize the supplies for the court, and how many governors does he appoint?
What picture of life does the text paint with the image of each one “under his own vine and under his own fig tree”?
The word חׇכְמָה (chokhmah, “wisdom”) appears in several fields in this chapter: what areas of knowledge does it cover in the description of Solomon?
Living in safety “under one's own vine” is an image of everyday peace: what would make your home or your neighborhood look more like this?
Why, according to Solomon, could David not build the temple, and what does Solomon ask of Hiram?
What kind of relationship is established between Hiram and Solomon, and what does it show about Israel's openness to neighboring peoples?
The word מַס (mas, “forced labor”) describes the system imposed on Israel: what human cost does the building of the temple bring, and how does this echo the warning of 1 Samuel 8?
Thousands work in shifts on the project under supervisors: how do you acknowledge the work of those who stay behind the scenes in the projects you take part in?
When does the building of the temple begin, according to the count in verse 1, and what curious detail does the text give about the noise of the work?
Why does the word of the LORD interrupt the description of the work, and on what does the promise to dwell among Israel depend?
The כְּרוּב (kerub, “cherubim”) dominate the Most Holy Place and the doors: what other texts of the Bible associate cherubim with God's presence, and what does this image suggest here?
The temple was assembled without the noise of tools on site: what might this detail inspire in the way you build important things, at home or at work?
How long does Solomon take to build his own house, and what other buildings does he put up?
The text records thirteen years for the palace right after the seven years for the temple: what comparison does the narrator seem to invite the reader to make?
The two עַמּוּד (‘ammud, “pillar”) receive the names Jachin and Boaz: what might it mean to give names to pillars at the entrance of the temple?
Hiram, the son of a widow, is remembered for his skill in working bronze: what ability of yours could you see as a gift in the service of something greater?
What was inside the ark, and what happens when the priests come out of the sanctuary?

The refrain “hear from heaven,” with שָׁמַיִם (shamayim, “heavens”), is repeated in the prayer: how does Solomon hold together God's presence in the house and the idea that even the highest heavens cannot contain Him?
What situations of crisis does Solomon list in his prayer, and what is asked of God in almost all of them?
Why does the prayer include the foreigner who comes from afar, and what does this say about the purpose of the temple?
Solomon admits that “there is no one who does not sin” in the middle of a dedication feast: how can this honesty shape the way you pray?
What promise and what warning does the LORD give Solomon in this second appearance?
Why does the text imagine foreigners passing by a ruined temple and asking the reason, and what does this scene foreshadow in Israel's history?
The verb בָּנָה (banah, “build”) is repeated in the list of Solomon's works: what does the chapter allow us to glimpse about the cost and manner of all this building?
Hiram is disappointed with the cities he receives and nicknames them Cabul: how do you make sure that what you offer others matches what you received from them?
Why does the queen of Sheba come to Jerusalem, and what does she see that leaves her breathless?
What purpose does the queen attribute to Solomon's reign, and how does this compare with the rest of the chapter, centered on wealth?
The זָהָב (zahav, “gold”) appears in almost everything the chapter describes: how should this splendor be read in light of the limits for kings in Deuteronomy 17:16-17?
The queen says she did not believe “until I came and saw with my own eyes”: what do you need to see for yourself before you trust?
What does Solomon do because of his foreign wives, and to what gods does he build altars?
The verb נָטָה (natah, “turn away, incline”) describes Solomon's heart: how did this turning happen little by little, according to the text, and not all at once?
Why is the division of the kingdom postponed until after Solomon and one tribe kept, and what does this reveal about the promise made to David?
What does Ahijah's gesture of tearing the new cloak into twelve pieces mean, and what conditions are given to Jeroboam?
Solomon's heart turned away “in his old age,” after a brilliant beginning: what helps you stay faithful throughout your whole life, and not only at the start?
What do the people ask of Rehoboam at Shechem, and what different advice does he receive from the elders and from the young men?
The verb יָעַץ (ya‘ats, “take counsel”) appears with Rehoboam and then with Jeroboam: what kind of counsel does each king follow, and where does it lead the two kingdoms?
What fear leads Jeroboam to make the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and what other episode of Israel's history do his words echo?
The elders say that if the king becomes “a servant to this people,” he will be served forever: in what position of leadership of yours could this idea change your attitudes?
What does the man of God announce against the altar at Bethel, and what happens to Jeroboam's hand?
The word דֶּרֶךְ (derekh, “way”) runs through the story of the man of God: what instruction did he have about the way, and what happens when he goes back by another?
How should we understand an account in which the prophet who lies survives and the one who was deceived dies? What does the text seem to want to teach by this?
The old prophet uses a supposed word from an angel to persuade the other: how do you evaluate spiritual guidance that contradicts what you already know clearly?
Why does Jeroboam send his wife in disguise to Shiloh, and how does Ahijah recognize her even without being able to see?
The verb קָבַר (qavar, “bury”) marks the exception in Jeroboam's house: why will only the boy Abijah receive burial and mourning?
What is the meaning of replacing Solomon's gold shields with bronze shields in Rehoboam's reign?
Ahijah accuses Jeroboam of having flung God “behind your back”: what have you been setting aside, out of sight, in your spiritual life?
What reforms does Asa carry out in Judah, and what does he do with his grandmother Maacah?
The formula “in the eyes of the LORD,” with עַיִן (‘ayin, “eye”), evaluates each king: what criterion does the book use to judge the kings, and why does it matter more than conquests?
How do you evaluate Asa's decision to use the temple treasures to buy Ben-hadad's help against Baasha?
The text says the high places were not removed, but Asa's heart was fully devoted to the LORD: how do you deal with areas that have not yet changed in a life that, on the whole, seeks God?
How many kings does Israel have in this chapter, and how does each one come to or lose the throne?
The verb חָטָא (chata', “sin”) also appears in the form “caused Israel to sin”: what special responsibility does the book attribute to the kings for the people's sin?
Why is Ahab's reign presented as worse than all the previous ones, and what role does the marriage with Jezebel play?
The rebuilding of Jericho fulfills an old word of Joshua at a terrible price: what warning do you draw from projects carried out without counting the cost to one's own family?
Where does the LORD tell Elijah to hide, how is he fed there, and why does he have to leave?
Elijah is sustained by a foreign אַלְמָנָה (’almanah, “widow”) from Zarephath: why is it significant that help comes from someone so vulnerable and from outside Israel?
How do the death and return to life of the boy change what the woman thinks about Elijah and about the word of the LORD?
The widow gives the little she has before seeing the result: in what situation have you been called to trust without guarantees?
Who is Obadiah, what did he do for the prophets, and why is he afraid to deliver Elijah's message?
The verb עָנָה (‘anah, “answer”) marks the challenge on Carmel: what does Baal's silence in the face of so much shouting highlight about the question “who is God?”?
Why does Elijah rebuild the altar with twelve stones and drench it with water before praying?
The chapter ends with the slaughter of the prophets of Baal at the Kishon: how should this violent ending be read in light of the rest of the Bible and of our time?
“How long will you waver between two opinions?”: in what decision of your life have you remained divided, without choosing?
What leads Elijah to flee to Beersheba and ask to die, and how is he cared for in the wilderness?
Elijah repeats twice that he has been “very zealous,” with the verb קָנָא (qana', “be zealous”): what does God's answer suggest about this zeal and about the idea of being alone?
Why is the LORD not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but makes Himself known in a gentle whisper, right after the fire on Carmel?
Before any word, the angel gives Elijah food and rest: what do you need to take care of in your body in order to keep going on the way?
What does Ben-hadad demand of Ahab in the first and second messages, and at what point does Ahab refuse to give in?
What do the Arameans think about the God of Israel being “a god of the hills,” and how does the LORD's answer correct this idea?
An anonymous נָבִיא (navi', “prophet”) appears several times beside Ahab: what do these nameless prophets do differently from Elijah, and why does the text include them?
“The one putting on his armor should not boast like one taking it off”: where have you been claiming victory too soon?
What does Ahab propose to Naboth, and why does Naboth refuse?
Naboth's כֶּרֶם (kerem, “vineyard”) was “the inheritance of my fathers”: what value did family land have in Israel, and why does this make the crime even more serious?
How does Jezebel use the law, fasting and false witnesses to kill Naboth, and who cooperates with the plan?
Why does the LORD postpone the punishment when Ahab humbles himself, and what does this say about the way God responds to repentance?
“Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?”: in what situations today can economic power trample those who have little, and what can you do about it?
What does Jehoshaphat ask for before going to war, and what do the four hundred prophets say with one voice?
Micaiah swears to say only what the LORD “says,” with the verb דָבַר (davar, “speak”): why does his first answer repeat the other prophets, and what makes the king suspicious?
How should we understand the vision of the heavenly council and the “lying spirit”? What questions does it raise about the responsibility of Ahab and his prophets?
Ahab disguises himself to escape Micaiah's announcement: what do the outcome of the battle and the detail of the dogs say about the prophetic word in the book?
Ahab says he hates Micaiah because he “never prophesies anything good about me”: do you tend to surround yourself only with voices that say what you want to hear?
